Look for predictors that carry the outcome rather than predict it

Source: R/leakage.R
mm_leakage.Rd

Three tiers, because they are three different findings and only one of them is settled by arithmetic.

Usage

mm_leakage(project, frame, y = NULL, min_overlap = 10L)

Arguments

project

A mm_project().

frame

The development rows, after eligibility. Not modified.

y

Optional 0/1 outcome for those rows, to avoid recomputing it.

min_overlap

Fewest rows with both values observed for a verdict of duplication. Below this an exact match carries too little information to separate a copy from a coincidence, so the predictor is left alone.

Value

A list of findings, each with tier, predictor, kind, n_compared, n_missing and detail.

Details

Tier 1, duplication. A predictor that reproduces the outcome on every eligible row, or its exact complement. There is no cohort in which that is a prediction, so it is an error.

Tier 2, categorical separation. Every observed level of a categorical predictor falls in one outcome class. That can be leakage and can equally be a small cohort, so it is reported for a human to settle.

Tier 3, numeric separation. A threshold exists that separates the classes completely. Same reasoning as tier 2.

A strong but non-deterministic association is not reported at all. A correlation is what a predictor is for.

What this cannot do is worth stating, because the gap is where published models go wrong: none of these tests says when a predictor was measured. A variable recorded after the outcome, a treatment chosen because of it, or a feature engineered from it can be weakly associated and still be leakage. Checking availability at the moment of prediction is the analyst's, and no comparison of columns can do it.
